Des hommes noirs brisent les tabous sur: Black men are breaking taboos around mental health, masculinity and silence in their communities.

La santé mentale au sein des communautés: Mental health in Black communities was the starting point for this article. Very quickly, it became clear that the focus had to be on Black men and their relationship to mental health.
Le constat, sans surprise : ils consulte: The finding, unsurprisingly: they seek help very rarely.
Au fil des entrevues, j’ai compris que l: Over the course of the interviews, I came to understand that the barriers to asking for help are not only individual. They stem from taboos within Black communities, from racism, from pressures tied to manliness, and from the lack of accessible role models. These barriers are rooted in a lack of positive representation, experiences of medical discrimination, and stereotypes that are still far too present in the way outsiders see us.
Cet article n’a pas la prétention d’expl: This article does not claim to explain or resolve anything. It seeks to open a space to break a little of the silence and to understand why some Black men think mental health is not for them.
« Les hommes ne pleurent pas. » Cette ph: “Men don’t cry.” This phrase, simple in appearance, carries the weight of a society that imposes expectations about what a man should be. In Black communities, mental health often remains a taboo, caught in the grip of toxic masculinity, stereotypes and a legacy of silence and resilience passed down from generation to generation. However, the barriers are beginning to crack, and spaces for speaking out are emerging to encourage Black men to break their silence and the clichés.
An evening in late March, in Blainville. Pouring rain did not stop about fifty people from taking their seats in a hushed room at the Grand Hotel Times to address a subject that is rarely talked about: men’s mental health.
Ils sont jeunes ou plus âgés, immigrants: They are young or older, immigrants or second-generation, professionals, students, sometimes fathers. They came to listen, some to speak, and all of them, above all, to understand the invisible weight they carry inside, that voice that keeps telling them: “It’s not for me.”
Sur scène, on s’affaire aux derniers pré: On stage, final preparations are under way to record an episode of the podcast État D’homme, hosted by Youvey Jean, a speaker committed to men’s well-being. Right away, he points out a statistic that is often overlooked: “Three out of four people who die by suicide in Canada are men.”
Des chiffres percutants publiés en 2022: Striking figures published in 2022 by the Institut national de santé publique du Québec (INSPQ) set the tone and underline the importance of the subject. According to the INSPQ, the suicide rate among men is three times higher than among women, and nearly one in 10 men experiences significant psychological distress.
Avec des statistiques aussi frappantes,: With statistics this striking, it quickly becomes clear that the mental health problems of Black men can no longer be ignored.
Youvey Jean, qui est âgé de 41 ans, est: Youvey Jean, who is 41, is joined on stage by Frantz-Daniel, a 38-year-old social services worker, and Jayden, an 18-year-old comedian and actor.
« Je suis au cégep. Et au cégep, la sant: “I’m in CEGEP. And in CEGEP, mental health doesn’t really exist. It’s just mental, that’s it.” A burst of laughter fills the room, lightening the atmosphere while introducing the subject they are about to discuss.
Les trois intervenants entament une disc: The three speakers begin a discussion on the effects of toxic masculinity on men’s mental well-being. Social pressure demands a posture, that of the invincible man, and it doesn’t spare “intimate, family or friendship relationships,” according to Youvey. “You have to be stoic, you have to be like Superman in any situation. But how do we live that in our relationships?” he asks.
Frantz-Daniel concède que le stéréotype: Frantz-Daniel concedes that the stereotype of the strong man has acted as a barrier for him in the past. “It affected me a bit. I find, on the contrary, that a man who cries or shows that vulnerability is showing a great strength,” he says, before explaining that the people around him have a lot to do with it. “I have key people I like to turn to, who give me resources and advice to help me get better aligned. That’s why the choice of the people around you matters,” he explains into the microphone.
Youvey, lui, a vécu une tout autre expér: Youvey, for his part, had a completely different experience when he was younger. “You can’t talk to your friends because they’ll make fun of you; you can’t talk to your family because they’ll think you’re crazy. And you don’t want to talk to women because you’re afraid they’ll find you too emotional and too weak.”
Avant de pouvoir accepter de l’aide, il: Before he could accept help, he had to unlearn what he had been taught since childhood. “A little girl falls, you comfort her. A little boy? You tell him to get up, not to cry. You push him to be tough, too early.”
À l’âge adulte, ces enseignements devien: In adulthood, these lessons become destructive. “You don’t cry over a breakup. You don’t cry over a job. You swallow everything. And over time, you end up thinking the problem is you. That you’re not good enough. That you’re useless.”
Son apparence imposante – 1,95 m pour 13: His imposing build – 1.95 m and 130 kg – also heightened this sense of having to be unshakeable. “I thought a big guy like me couldn’t be emotional. It was a real block,” he acknowledges.

« Chaque échec que tu vis, tu dois le vi: “Every failure you go through, you have to go through in silence, and it can hurt you enormously.” He hints that this inability to open up can lead someone to think about suicide. “You don’t want to talk about it, so you start thinking: ‘I’d be better off if I wasn’t on this earth anymore.’” His testimony is raw, intimate, and it resonates in the room.
Avec une grande simplicité, il résume :: With great simplicity, he sums it up: “When your body is sick, you go to the doctor. Why not do the same for your mind?” A question that launches the debate on accepting mental health as a public health issue, just like any other illness.
Quand les micros se ferment et que l’enr: When the microphones are switched off and the podcast recording ends, the room comes alive. A buzz fills the air, conversations fly. Everyone digests the words they’ve heard as they head to the buffet. In the line is one of the few women present, Manuela Théodore Rigaud, a lecturer.
Si les témoignages des intervenants soul: While the speakers’ testimonies underline the importance of deconstructing stereotypes tied to masculinity, Manuela Théodore Rigaud, for her part, insists on the need to redefine how mental health is viewed in Black communities.
À la question « En fait-on assez pour le: Asked, “Are we doing enough for Black men in the field of mental health?”, she answers bluntly: “I don’t think the question is ‘Are we doing enough?’ but rather ‘Are we doing it well enough for them to understand that the message is for them too?’”
Selon elle, il ne suffit pas de parler a: In her view, it isn’t enough to talk to Black men about psychological disorders. First we have to reframe the codes, deconstruct an inherited notion of manliness and break invisible chains: cultural, religious, historical. “Many people consider that mental health is for certain cultures, including Caucasians, and not for people of colour,” she observes.
Psychoéducatrice de profession et co-cré: A psychoeducator by profession and co-creator of the podcast Afro-descendants : Démystifions notre bien-être, Manuela observes an overvaluing of resilience in Black communities, inherited from the colonial past, in which Black men were reduced to their physical strength.
« L’histoire fait en sorte que l’idée qu: “History has made the idea of not being well mentally impossible, incompatible with our identity,” she explains. “There are people who think it can’t be, because if your basic needs are met, you have no right to explore whether things are going well or badly, because we’ve learned to survive. And that’s a reality for Black people.”
Avancer est donc devenu un réflexe. Pour: Pushing forward has therefore become a reflex. Yet the numbers tell a different story. A survey <l1>conducted in 2021 by the Mental Health Commission of Canada among 328 Black Canadians found that 35.4%</l1> of respondents were experiencing considerable psychological distress.
<l1>En 2023, 63,3 % des personnes noires: <l1>In 2023, 63.3% of Black people in Canada</l1> reported that they perceived their mental health, by their own assessment, as “excellent” or “very good” – a rate higher than the national average, according to Statistics Canada. This statistical paradox is puzzling: does it reflect real well-being, or a deeper difficulty in recognizing and expressing psychological distress?

Selon Manuela, la peur d’être étiqueté c: According to Manuela, the fear of being labelled “crazy” or “mentally ill” keeps many men from deciding to turn to a mental health professional.
Jennifer A. Burnham, une des organisatri: Jennifer A. Burnham, one of the conference organizers, knows something about that. She speaks of the difficulty of convincing men to take part in such an event and the discomfort it creates for them. “They told me: ‘It’s not for me, I’m not crazy.’”
Pour Youvey Jean, des facteurs religieux: For Youvey Jean, religious factors also play a role in the distance people in Black communities put between themselves and mental health. “I grew up in a very devout family, and we were told that mental health was either a White people’s illness or a matter of evil spirits,” he says. This inner conflict paralyzed him for a long time. “For me, mental health was a right I wasn’t allowed to have,” he confides.
Un discours que Melchi connaît bien, lui: Melchi knows this discourse well, too: “No matter what happens, the good Lord will save you. We have that mentality a lot.” Born in the 1980s into a Haitian family, he long thought mental health wasn’t part of his world. “You’re not allowed to cry. Not allowed to show weakness,” he sums up. Today, looking back, he understands that asking for help is not an admission of fragility. “I went through some really low moments and I realized that mental health is important.” But how many, like him, come to that realization?
Assis à ses côtés, Evans, venu également: Seated beside him, Evans, who also came to attend the conference, nods. For him, this evening is a breath of fresh air. “In our community, it’s still taboo. As a man, you’re supposed to be strong,” he says quietly. “Someone who grew up with that mentality won’t necessarily go looking for help. He’ll try to find help on his own, by other means that can be harmful.” Drugs, alcohol, isolation – so many escapes to mask distress.
Aujourd’hui, Youvey Jean veut briser le:
Today, Youvey Jean wants to break the cycle of silence. His podcast <l1>État d’homme</l1> was born out of urgency: “I’m not a specialist. I’m just someone who has lived through mental health difficulties and wants to offer others an anchor point,” he says. “The goal is to make men aware of the tool that mental health can be.”

The podcast is aimed at people of all backgrounds and all generations, no matter where they live. It resonates beyond borders, with Youvey Jean having listeners as far away as Côte d’Ivoire.
Le projet agit aussi comme une boussole: The project also acts as a compass for his own balance. “It helps me keep working on myself. By doing research, I discover things. And you’re never done working on yourself. It’s a way of maintaining my mental health.”
Pour ouvrir davantage d’espaces de parol: To open up more spaces for speaking, Youvey is considering creating a monthly discussion circle for men. It’s an idea he’s already testing with those close to him, in informal settings conducive to trust. “We have to let go of machismo, of toxic masculinity. You can be strong, but also vulnerable, emotional, and able to seek support when things aren’t going well.” In Montréal, other initiatives pursue the same goal. The Black Healing Center, created by and for Black people, is developing mental health projects designed specifically for men. Among them are wellness events in familiar places such as barbershops. “A lot of men came,” says founder and executive director Samantha Nyinawumuntu. “They’re open to talking, but you have to create spaces that speak to them. And ideally, those spaces should be designed and run by Black men for Black men.”
Selon Youvey Jean, ce n’est que le début: According to Youvey Jean, this is only the beginning of a larger movement. “There’s still a lot of work to do, both in the communities and in the associations and institutions that support Black populations.” <l1>In 2024, Canada allocated $4 million over two years to the Mental Health of Black Canadians Fund</l1>, intended to support grassroots solutions nationwide and to fund culturally adapted projects. However, despite these efforts, turning to a mental health professional is not automatic for many Black men.
Bien que les recherches sur la santé men: Although research on mental health is growing, data specifically on Black men is still far too scarce. Yet the findings are there: according to the Government of Canada website, <l1>anti-Black racism directly contributes to depressive symptoms, thereby affecting the mental health, on a daily basis, of Black people who are exposed to stress, precarity and racism</l1>.
Pour Sophie Annabelle Barateau, psycholo: For Sophie Annabelle Barateau, an anti-racist clinical psychologist of Haitian origin, failing to take these racial issues into account when caring for patients from Black communities can also be an obstacle and a source of bias in health care.
« Il y a certaines personnes qui apparti: “There are some people in the Black community who will receive different treatment simply because they are Black,” she says.
Il est donc impératif, selon elle, de fo: It is therefore imperative, she says, to train health professionals to be anti-racist. She also raises awareness among her colleagues through conferences so that they know how to work with racialized people. One of the main levers available to encourage Black men to seek help, she explains, also lies in sharing positive collective experiences. But she admits that, beyond cultural taboos, there are real obstacles to accessing care: wait times, the cost of services, and the lack of Black representation among professionals in the health care system.
Melchi, lui, estime que, si beaucoup d’h: Melchi, for his part, believes that if many Black men still think mental health is not for them, it’s because of a lack of information. So for him, events like the evening he is attending tonight are crucial. “We’ve reached that point. This needs to happen more often,” he insists.
